title: Most of our waking hours
hookLine: traditions have plenty to say about work, the place so much of life happens

lines: AN ALARM. A SHIFT. THE DISHES.
cards: An alarm before it's light. A commute, or a walk from the bed to the kitchen table. Then the hours: the shift, the inbox, the diapers, the field, the classroom, the delivery route, the dishes.
Tally the waking hours of a week and see where they go. If the answer is work, paid or unpaid, then work is where a life is mostly lived.
And if the great questions only show up in the quiet hours, they'll miss most of the day. Today begins sixty days on work. First: karma yoga.

teach.b: Start where the last block ended. In The Prophet, Kahlil Gibran has a plowman ask about work, and the answer bridges love and labor in five words: “Work is love made visible.”
Bake bread without care, Gibran says, and you bake a bitter bread that feeds only half a hunger. The care goes in with the flour.

teach.h: ACT, AND LET GO OF THE FRUIT.
teach.b: Second, the Bhagavad Gita. On a battlefield, the warrior Arjuna wants to lay down his bow and walk away from what he's been given to do. Krishna answers that his concern is with the action alone, never with its fruits.
Hindu teachers call this karma yoga: doing the work fully, while letting go of how it turns out. Third, a kitchen.

teach.h: GOD AMONG THE POTS AND PANS.
teach.b: A lay brother in a French monastery, remembered as Brother Lawrence, worked among pots and pans.

In the letters and conversations gathered after him, he says he felt as close to God in the clatter of the kitchen as on his knees at prayer. Fourth, what these voices share, without becoming one voice.
None treats work as the thing that gets in the way of a spiritual life. Gibran sees love in it. The Gita sees a path.
They differ on what work is for, but each puts the great questions where the hours actually go.
Next come Jewish and Christian voices: a garden, sweat, a sabbath, a craftsman, an ant.

how: Traditions bring faith into daily work in their own ways: some Hindus practice karma yoga, offering action without clinging to its results, and some Christians follow Brother Lawrence's practice of the presence of God during ordinary tasks.

in The Prophet, answering a plowman's question about work.

he said he felt as close to God among the pots and pans as at prayer.
Krishna tells Arjuna to care only about results

games.q: you're Arjuna on the battlefield, ready to lay down your bow and walk away from your work. what does Krishna tell you?
o: walk away; work distracts from the spirit.
act, and let go of the fruits.
act only when you're sure of the outcome.
games.why: in the Gita, Krishna says Arjuna's concern is with the action alone, never with its fruits: the root of karma yoga.

practice: Choose one task you do so often you've stopped seeing it, folding laundry, packing a lunch, opening the store, and walk through it slowly in your mind as if watching a stranger: the hands, the tools, the small decisions.
Then follow it outward to whoever eats, wears or uses what you do, and notice one thing about it you'd stopped noticing. If you pray, you can offer that work in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Karma yoga. The path the Gita describes: doing the work fully, while letting go of how it turns out. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, from Hindu teaching: action, work; in the Gita, work done without clinging to its fruit.
